articles.title: World Insights: War shrine tributes on surrender day reveal Japan's lingering militarist obsession
articles.body:
TOKYO, Aug. 16 (Xinhua) -- Aug. 15 marks the 81st anniversary of Japan's unconditional surrender in World War II. On the day, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi sent a ritual offering to the notorious war-linked Yasukuni Shrine, while making no mention of "remorse" in her first war memorial address.
Analysts believe Japan's ruling authorities are persistently pushing to accelerate military expansion and rearmament and promoting right-wing historical views and narratives of "regional threats," with increasingly evident characteristics of "neo-militarism." They warn that today's Japan bears a striking resemblance to the Japan that embarked on a path of aggressive war in the past; if left unchecked, this trajectory poses a serious threat to regional peace and stability, and the international community should remain highly vigilant.
NO SIGN OF REMORSE
On Saturday, Takaichi made a "tamagushi" ritual offering to the Yasukuni Shrine, a symbol of the country's militarism and wartime aggression, in her capacity as president of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). Before attending the National Memorial Service for the War Dead, she turned toward the shrine across the road and bowed twice, clapped twice and bowed once from the parking area of Nippon Budokan hall, in an apparent act of Shinto worship.
Meanwhile, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and several other cabinet ministers showed up at the shrine earlier Saturday, marking the seventh consecutive year that sitting Japanese ministers have paid respects there on Aug. 15. LDP Secretary-General Shunichi Suzuki, other top ruling party executives, and a nonpartisan group of dozens of lawmakers also visited the shrine.
In her speech at the annual memorial held in Tokyo, Takaichi neither mentioned Japan's wars of aggression against its Asian neighbors nor expressed remorse or apology for the suffering they caused. She even altered a phrase traditionally used by previous prime ministers, changing "must never repeat the horrors of war" into "The horrors of war must never be repeated." Japanese media pointed out that the revised wording deliberately obscures the subject responsible for the war, thereby avoiding reflection on Japan's wartime aggression.
This is not the first time Takaichi has employed such rhetorical ambiguity. In speeches earlier this month at ceremonies commemorating the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, she merely stated that Japan "is adhering to the Three Non-Nuclear Principles," while remaining vague about whether her government would continue to uphold them. Some Japanese media criticized the ambiguity as evidence that the prime minister has failed to genuinely learn from history.
Takaichi has long been associated with controversial positions on historical issues. In 1994, she publicly questioned the Murayama government's apology and remorse over Japan's wartime aggression, arguing that a prime minister could not apologize on behalf of the Japanese people. In a television program in 2002, she described Japan's wartime actions as a "war for self-preservation and self-defense," drawing sharp criticism. She has also published articles on her official website endorsing the right-wing "Greater East Asia War" historical narrative and promoting the prewar Imperial Rescript on Education, a document widely associated with militarist ideology.
Takakage Fujita, secretary-general of the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement, said the ruling authorities not only lack reflection on Japan's aggression but also display a wartime logic disturbingly similar to that of the political leaders who led Japan into war more than 80 years ago.
Anatoly Koshkin, executive council member of the Russian Association of World War II Historians, said the ideological poison of militarism continues to spread in Japanese society; influenced by right-wing propaganda, many in the younger generation, who have no firsthand memories of the horrors of war, hope to see Japan's return as a major military power.
RAPID REMILITARIZATION
The Japanese government has long sought to bolster the country's military capabilities, gradually chipping away at the military constraints imposed by the postwar pacifist constitution and steadily hollowing out the long-standing principle of "exclusively defense-oriented policy."
Since Takaichi took office, her government has only hit the accelerator on military buildup.
At the institutional level, the Takaichi administration has been taking a series of aggressive moves, from seeking to revise the Three Non-Nuclear Principles when updating the country's three key security documents by the end of this year, to speeding up efforts to amend the pacifist constitution, aiming to make headway on a constitutional amendment proposal before next year's Liberal Democratic Party convention.
Meanwhile, a reform to centralize the country's intelligence apparatus is underway, including the establishment of a national intelligence agency, to tighten control over public opinion and facilitate military expansion.
In terms of military deployment and operations, the Takaichi administration has put offensive weapons into actual service, deploying long-range missiles with so-called "enemy base strike capabilities" in Japan for the first time and conducting the first test-firing of U.S.-made Tomahawk cruise missiles.
It has also accelerated efforts to expand the Self-Defense Forces' overseas presence, sending a large contingent of combat personnel to the Philippines for joint military drills for the first time, and is vigorously developing "new ways of warfare" and working to enhance sustained combat capabilities.
On the fiscal front, the Japanese government has significantly increased defense spending. A supplementary budget for fiscal 2025 allowed Japan to hit its target of raising defense-related spending to 2 percent of gross domestic product two years ahead of schedule, and the surge has continued unabated. With the initial defense budget for fiscal 2026 having reached a new record high, the defense budget request for fiscal 2027 is reportedly set to climb even further.
Economically, the Japanese authorities are trying to turn the defense industry into a new pillar for reviving the country's economy. In April this year, the Takaichi government revised the "three principles on transfer of defense equipment and technology" and their implementation guidelines, allowing the export of lethal weapons in principle, and thereby opening up markets for Japan's military industry.
Meanwhile, the country's 2026 defense white paper significantly expanded discussion of reinforcing defense production and technological bases, touting the defense business as a contributor to "Japan's economic growth."
In manipulating public opinion and perceptions, the Takaichi administration has not only continued to downplay, deny, and whitewash the history of Japanese aggression, but has also hyped up alleged "security threats" from neighboring countries, particularly the so-called "China threat," to pave the way for military expansion.
Takaichi has publicly claimed that a "Taiwan contingency" could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" that could allow Japan to exercise the right of collective self-defense, and has cast China as "an unprecedented and the greatest strategic challenge."
Australian business strategy consultant Antony Hing said Japan is "very rapidly" shifting away from its pacifist constitution, and it could be in breach of its international legal obligations in acting the way it's acting.
Ling Tek Soon, senior lecturer at the Institute of China Studies of the University of Malaya, said that Japan is constantly pushing beyond the institutional boundaries of the postwar order, departing from the "peaceful nation" identity and development path it has long professed.
HISTORY'S WARNING
Japanese historians, including Masahiro Yamazaki, have pointed out that Japan's current political, military, economic and ideological trajectory bears striking similarities to the path the country took prior to World War II.
Following the Meiji Restoration, Japan gradually embarked on a course of militarist expansion abroad. During the 1930s, it responded to economic crisis with military buildup and external aggression. Military leaders, politicians and powerful business interests formed close alliances to stoke fears of "external threats" and "existential crisis" to mobilize public support for war. National resources were concentrated in the military sector, benefiting the military establishment and large industrial conglomerates while ordinary people bore the economic burden and ultimately became victims of war.
Today, a similar scenario is playing out again. Faced with domestic challenges such as prolonged economic stagnation, Japan's right-wing conservative forces view "breaking free from the post-war order" and becoming a "normal country" as a supposed way out.
Government resources continue to shift toward defense, with military expansion presented as a means of stimulating economic growth. At the same time, narratives emphasizing "external threats," denying historical aggression and reviving prewar militarist ideology are increasingly used for political and social mobilization, leading to a resurgence of militarism in Japan.
These trends have sparked strong protests and heightened vigilance among the Japanese public.
Yamazaki warned that the government's persistent emphasis on "external threats" could easily steer Japan into war once again. Akira Yamada, professor at Meiji University, said Japan's continued military buildup risks fueling a regional arms race that could become increasingly difficult to reverse once established.
Critics also argue that Japan's remilitarization carries growing domestic costs. As defense spending reaches record levels, military contractors have reaped substantial profits while social welfare and other livelihood-related expenditures face mounting pressure. The result, they say, is worsening public finances and increasing hardship for ordinary citizens.
Atsushi Koketsu, professor emeritus at Yamaguchi University, argued that the government's push for remilitarization comes at the expense of public welfare. "It is fundamentally wrong to place people's livelihoods in insecurity in exchange for so-called national security," he said.
Kim Joo-Yong, professor of history and culture at South Korea's Wonkwang University, said the truly responsible path for Japan is to confront its history and draw lessons from it. "Countries in the region, together with peace-loving forces within Japan, should unite in opposing militarism," he said. ■

articles.title: Russian strikes kill Ukrainian woman as NATO jet downs drone over Romania
articles.body:
Ukraine targets Moscow in mass drone attack as Russia bombards Kyiv
Russian authorities report 201 Ukrainian drones downed overnight in the Moscow region during the escalating conflict.
At least one person has been killed in and three others were wounded in a Ukrainian drone barrage targeting Moscow, a local official said, as Russia bombarded Kyiv with ballistic missiles.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin wrote on social media early Sunday that the city had been targeted with 600 drones and that “201 drones were destroyed in Moscow region.”

Andrei Vorobyov, Governor of Moscow Oblast, wrote on Telegram that an 83-year-old man was killed after a drone hit a private home.
At least three other people were killed in attacks on Russia’s southern Rostov region, which borders Ukraine, according to regional authorities.
The drone assault comes after Ukrainian authorities said at least one person was killed and seven others were wounded in Russian air attacks.
A woman was killed and six others were wounded in a missile and drone attack on Kryvyi Rig, the hometown of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in central Ukraine, the region’s governor said.
Officials in the capital said Kyiv was “under ballistic missile attack” late on Saturday, with at least one person wounded and fires sparked at non-residential sites in the Obolonsky and Holosiivskyi districts.
Separately, Romania’s Defence Ministry reported on Sunday that a Spanish F-18 fighter jet pilot on a NATO air policing mission to Romania had shot down a drone illegally breaching its national airspace.
It is the fourth drone shot down in Romania this year.
Romania’s Defence Ministry wrote on social media that the drone came from neighbouring country Moldova.
“The surveillance systems of the Ministry of National Defense detected the intrusion of an aerial target into national airspace, coming from the Republic of Moldova,” it said in a statement.
Defence Minister Radu Miruta congratulated the pilots and military personnel on what he called “a successful mission.”
In July, a Romanian jet shot down a suspected Russian drone, and in May a stray drone injured two people in the Romanian city of Galati when it collided with a building.
Romania shares a 634km (394-mile) border with Ukraine and has repeatedly seen Russian drones breaching its airspace as Moscow escalates its bombing campaign against Ukrainian civilian and military infrastructure.
Escalating long-range strikes
Russia has maintained near-daily missile and drone strikes across Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in early 2022, with areas far from the front lines frequently coming under attack.
The war’s impact has also spread to key regional shipping lanes, with reports of mines and unmanned sea drones found floating in the Black Sea.
Civilian casualties in Ukraine hit their highest level since 2022 this July, with at least 437 killed and 2,610 injured, according to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted military, industrial and logistical facilities deep inside Russia, arguing its strikes are a response to Moscow’s ongoing bombardment of Ukrainian towns and infrastructure.

articles.title: Marco Rubio has unique power to promote peace in the world. Why isn’t he doing his job? | Simon Tisdall
articles.body:
Viewed from the state department in Washington DC, the world is on fire – but record heatwaves are not to blame. The unresolved Iran war has badly burned Donald Trump. His military campaign conclusively failed, energy and food prices are still rising, and a Republican rout in November’s midterm elections looms. Humiliatingly, Israel this week flatly rejected his latest Gaza peace proposals, days after Trump congratulated himself on a “historic breakthrough”. In Europe, Russia’s attacks on Nato allies grow increasingly brazen, threatening a wider escalation. The Ukraine war, which Trump vowed to end, is now well into its fifth year, with civilians on both sides caught in the killing fields. And these are just the bigger firestorms. There are plenty more.
Rarely has the need for effective, professional diplomacy been more pressing. So step forward Marco Rubio, US secretary of state and chief American diplomat. These are challenges that, if successfully tackled, could propel the 55-year-old son of Cuban immigrants and the former US senator for Florida into pole position in the 2028 Republican presidential nomination race. Here is a chance for Rubio to defy critics who dismiss him as a lickspittle and Trump dogsbody, and transform himself into respected global statesman. His boss mocked him as “little Marco” and a “loser” when they were election rivals in 2016. (Rubio called him a conman.) Now is Rubio’s opportunity to go big, be brave and prove he’s a winner.
Or maybe not.
Rubio is unlike recent US secretaries of state – heavyweights such as Hillary Clinton and Antony Blinken, or John Kerry, famed for his high-energy shuttle diplomacy. Rubio has little time for “peace processes”. Instead, he projects brute US power to impose take-it-or-leave-it “solutions” that advance US interests, as defined by Trump. It’s a modern form of imperialism. Target countries have a choice: become client states, like Venezuela and, prospectively, Cuba and Greenland, or be crushed. In Iran, the policy is not regime change, let alone democratic renewal. It’s regime compliance. Rubio behaves less like a peace-broker, more like a pith-helmeted colonial viceroy demanding fealty from obsequious satraps.
Speaking in Munich in February, Rubio aired his hawkishly retro doctrine of US primacy. He lamented the decline of “the great western empires … accelerated by godless communist revolutions and anti-colonial uprisings” and warned Europe faced “civilisational erasure”. The US didn’t want milksop allies “shackled by guilt and shame” about their imperial past, he said. “We want allies who are proud of their culture and heritage … and who, together with us, are willing and able to defend it.” Here was a familiar assertion of US hegemony, but one stripped of bogus altruism and pretence. It sounded a death knell for diplomacy. Trump has attacked eight countries in the past year. Cuba, Rubio’s obsession, could be next.
Rubio’s reluctance to get personally involved in peacemaking may be partly explained by his other, contradictory role, as Trump’s national security adviser. He has accepted the White House’s outsourcing of negotiations over Ukraine and Palestine to amateur envoys of limited ability – namely Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and business crony Steve Witkoff. Broadly speaking, Rubio has steered clear of direct involvement in the Iran talks, too, leaving JD Vance, the vice-president and his main potential rival in 2028, to take the flak. Rubio’s arm’s length approach smacks of calculation. Or maybe he’s just out of his depth. Maybe he has no clear idea what he, Marco, really thinks about any of these issues and simply does Trump’s erratic bidding.
This perception of a political chameleon lacking firm principles, consistent opinions and a strong moral compass is reinforced by his record. His biographer, Manuel Roig-Franzia, believes Rubio’s personal and political slipperiness – he once became a Mormon, then reverted to Catholicism – is rooted in a childhood need to belong, to be on the winning side, no matter the price. Senator Rubio was a China hawk. Now he toes Trump’s ingratiating line on Beijing. He used to castigate Russia; now he’s an appeaser. He championed overseas assistance but, in office, has gutted USAID and seeks to dismantle the international criminal court, a keystone of global order. He blasted Barack Obama’s Iran nuclear deal. Now he backs an accord that would offer additional concessions to Tehran. Accused by the Vatican of waging an immoral, unjust war, he travelled to Rome and set the pope straight.
The irony, or tragedy, of the Rubio conundrum is he has the power to do great good, if only he would stand up and be counted. Russia’s Vladimir Putin, losing on the battlefield and at home, is weaker than at any time since 2022. Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy is short of missile interceptors, soldiers and political support. A ceasefire deal freezing the conflict is there for the making by the only country – the US – that can meaningfully squeeze both sides. Likewise, in Israel, the architect of the Gaza genocide and disastrous wars with Hamas, Iran and Hezbollah – Benjamin Netanyahu – faces defeat in October’s elections. Here’s a rare opportunity to quietly shelve Trump’s Board of Peace idiocies, halt Jewish settler violence in the West Bank and make a fresh, inclusive start based on UN resolutions.
Rubio could also do the Middle East, the global economy, American consumers and himself a power of good by taking charge of moribund peace talks with Iran and resuscitating the June memorandum of understanding that Tehran insists is the only route out of the strait of Hormuz logjam. In doing so, Rubio would have the enthusiastic backing of most Americans, European and Gulf state governments, energy producers and businesses, and Maga supporters who rightly fear Trump has dragged the US into another forever war. Even Trump may be grateful. He knows he’s in a hole. He needs someone to dig him out.
The fact that Rubio, despite his ostensibly uniquely powerful position, is unlikely to do any of the above marks him out as the most dangerous man in the US administration after Trump himself. He is dangerous because he enables and facilitates Trump’s worst instincts – and neglects his duty. He is dangerous because he provides pseudo-intellectual respectability to far-right fantasies about unfettered US supremacy. More so than the impetuous Vance, indulging in puerile name-calling on social media, and the “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth, a ranting ultra-nationalist, Rubio is dangerous because he can look and sound reasonable. He stands a fair chance of becoming Trump’s chosen successor and heir to the Maga brand.
Maybe, before that happens, he will change again. Maybe he will rediscover a few principles, find a diplomatic backbone, extinguish a few fires. He has shown repeatedly that his views are infinitely fungible. Rubio could yet do great things. Or he could become a problem as great or greater than Trump.
- 
  Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

articles.title: Troops from North Korea to boost Russia's Ukraine forces
articles.body:
Troops from North Korea to boost Russia's Ukraine forces
August 16, 2026
In late 2024, North Korea sent troops to help defend the Kursk region of Russia from Ukraine. International officials estimate that 14,000-15,000 North Korean troops were initially deployed to assist Russia in its war in Ukraine..
Now, Ukrainian and international intelligence agencies suspect that North Korea is planning to send an additional 30,000-50,000 troops to Russia. Ukrainian officials have also stated that North Korean ballistic missiles are being fired from Russia.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has raised concerns that North Korea's improved combat and weapons experience could pose a security threat to Ukraine, as well as the Asia-Pacific region.
Defense in Russia
Observers have had mixed responses to Zelenskyy's remarks. Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military and political expert at the Ukrainian Center for Security Studies, told DW that new troops from North Korea would likely be used to secure Russia's border territories. Aside from remaining in Kursk, North Korean soldiers could also help secure southwestern Vornezh.
"These forces could free up Russian occupational forces," Kovalenko said. "Russia would then be able to deploy around 15,000 troops to battles along front lines in Vovchansk, Kharkiv, Sumy or even Chernihiv."
Kovalenko does not expect North Korean troops to fight on Ukrainian territory.
The Russian military analyst Ruslan Leviev agrees. "It's one thing to recapture Russian territory," he told DW, "and an entirely different thing to be present on internationally recognized Ukrainian territory, taking part in a war of aggression."
"Diplomatically speaking," he said, "those are two entirely different concepts."
Russia not outgunned
Leviev said he had not seen concrete evidence of a noteworthy North Korean presence in Russia. He said Moscow had enough troops available without having to draw foreign soldiers into the fight.
"If you look at the front line, you can see that Russia's forces have been fairly active since mid-July," Leviev said. "That's a clear sign they still have enough forces."
Estimates by the economist Janis Kluge, of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), back this up. "While Russia's recruitment campaign has shown signs of strain this year, regional spending figures indicate that Russia is still recruiting around 1,000 contract soldiers each day," he recently wrote in a report.
Intelligence on North Korea's short- and medium-range ballistic systems, the KN-23 and KN-24, is far less speculative. Ukraine's Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) states that North Korea has delivered 148 KN-23 and KN-24 missiles since 2025.
In July, Zelenskyy said one such missile had struck a home near Ukraine's Kryvyi Rih, killing two parents and three children.
The HUR recently reported that a North Korean missile unit was deploying to Russia's Voronezh region, where it could be equipped with 120 ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy has taken this as indication that Russia's strategic reserve is depleted.
Kovalenko has come to a different conclusion. Instead of having run out of reserves, he said, he believes that Russia is looking to launch a higher number of missiles "to spread more terror."
'Instruments of terror'
Ukrainian military sources say North Korean missiles are similar to Russia's Iskander missiles, but with a greater payload, longer range and lower accuracy.
The military expert Yuri Fyodorov calls North Korea's missiles "instruments of terror." He told DW that "it is very difficult to hit a small target with North Korean weapons." He said he believed that Russia had deliberately targeted residential areas with these missiles.
Like the Russian Iskander 9M723, KN-23 and KN-24 missiles can only be stopped by US-made Patriot air-defense systems, which Ukraine has run critically low on.
Leviev said ballistic missiles would play a key role in this phase of the war. As Ukraine's stockpiles run low, he said, it will become a growing priority to Russia to keep a steady supply.
This summer, Leviev said, he has seen Russia launch far more ballistic missiles than in previous years. Should Russia's missile supply run low by winter, he said, "there will still be North Korea reserves, to make sure Ukraine cannot catch its breath."
No turning point
None of the experts DW spoke with believes that North Korea's involvement will bring about a turning point in Russia's war with Ukraine.
Jenny Town, of the US-based Foreign Policy Research Institute, said the time had passed for North Korea's involvement to make a significant difference. Instead, she said, Russia and North Korea have established a mutually beneficial partnership that is only likely to deepen through the course of the war with Ukraine.
Kovalenko also doesn't expect Russia to make substantial territorial gains along the front lines, but he is concerned about the upcoming winter. "October, November and December could become very trying for Ukraine," he said.
Russian forces could benefit from a possible new military call up, from freeing up fighters it replaces with North Korean troops and from a further stream of ballistic missiles. "That would be no good for the course of the war, and for Ukraine's war interests," Fyodorov said.
This article was originally written in Russian.

articles.title: Over the past 24 hours, 212 combat engagements occurred at the front, while Russia dropped 312 guided aerial bombs — General Staff
articles.body:
Over the past 24 hours, 212 combat engagements occurred at the front, while Russia dropped 312 guided aerial bombs — General Staff
Kyiv • UNN
Over the past 24 hours, 212 combat engagements were recorded at the front. The Russians carried out 99 airstrikes, dropping 312 guided aerial bombs.
During the past day, August 15, 212 combat engagements were recorded at the front. Russian occupiers carried out 99 airstrikes, during which they dropped 312 guided aerial bombs. This was reported by UNN, citing the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Details
In addition, the Russians deployed 11,235 kamikaze drones and carried out 3,122 strikes on populated areas and positions of Ukrainian troops, 64 of them using multiple-launch rocket systems.
The enemy shelled the populated areas of Korenok, Sopych, Bachivsk, Neskuchne, Bezsalivka, Rohizne, Ryzhivka, Hirky, Ulanove, Volfyne in Sumy region; and Khrinivka and Mykolaivka in Chernihiv region. Korenok and Ulanove came under airstrikes.
Over the past day, the aviation, missile forces and artillery of the Defense Forces struck 12 areas where enemy personnel were concentrated, seven artillery systems and one control post for unmanned aerial vehicles.
On the North Slobozhanskyi and Kursk fronts, our defenders stopped four enemy assaults over the past day. At the same time, the aggressor carried out 49 strikes on the positions of Ukrainian troops and populated areas.
On the South Slobozhanskyi front, Ukrainian units repelled five enemy attacks. The invaders attempted to advance near Vovchanski Khutory and toward the populated areas of Zybine, Anyskine and Okhrimivka.
On the Kupiansk front, the enemy conducted 10 offensive actions toward Radkivka and Kurylivka.
Attempts to penetrate the Ukrainian defenses were repelled on the Lyman front, where the occupiers attacked nine times toward the populated areas of Cherneshchyna, Novyi Myr, Drobysheve, Lyman and Dibrova, and near the populated areas of Ridkodub and Novoselivka.
On the Sloviansk front, the enemy carried out 21 assault actions in the areas of the populated areas of Riznykivka, Kryva Luka and Zakitne, and toward Rai-Oleksandrivka and Pyskynivka.
On the Kramatorsk front, the Russian invaders conducted no offensive actions.
Twenty-eight attacks were recorded on the Kostiantynivka front. The invaders conducted assault actions in the areas of the populated areas of Kostiantynivka, Ivanopillia, Illinivka, Novoselivka, Sofiivka and Rusyn Yar, and toward the populated areas of Vilne, Stepanivka, Novopavlivka and Kucheriv Yar.
The enemy carried out 34 attacks on the Pokrovsk front. The occupiers attempted to advance in the areas of the populated areas of Vasylivka, Udachne, Kotlyne and Novopidhორodne, and toward the populated areas of Bilytske, Novyi Donbas, Shevchenko, Novohryshyne, Serhiivka and Novopavlivka.
On the Oleksandrivka front, the invaders carried out two attacks toward the populated areas of Oleksandrohrad and Rybne.
On the Hulyaipole front, the occupiers attacked the positions of our defenders six times. The enemy attempted to advance toward the populated areas of Charivne, Novoselivka and Tsvitkove, and in the area of Bilohiria.
On the Orikhiv front, our defenders stopped three attempts by the enemy to advance toward Stepnohirsk and Plavni, and in the area of Plavni.
On the Dnipro front, the enemy conducted no assault actions over the past day.
Over the past day, Russian invader casualties amounted to 1,510 personnel. Also destroyed or disabled were one tank, seven armored combat vehicles, 75 artillery systems, eight multiple-launch rocket systems, two air defense systems, 16 ground robotic systems, 1,920 unmanned aerial vehicles, 476 motor vehicles and seven pieces of the enemy's special equipment.

articles.title: Drone Attacks Spark Large Fires at Wildberries Hubs Near Moscow
articles.body:
A large-scale fire broke out at a massive Wildberries logistics complex in the Moscow region early Sunday morning, Aug. 16, following a reported drone attack.
Astra Telegram channel reported that the blaze engulfed the Wildberries facility in the village of Koledino, near Podolsk. Spanning over 200,000 square meters (77,200 square feet), the Koledino site is reportedly the largest warehouse operated by the e-commerce giant.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Astra also reported that a second facility, the Severnoye Domodedovo multimodal logistics complex in Domodedovo, was also on fire.
The fires follow a mass drone attack on the Russian capital region. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin stated on Telegram that Russian air defenses had intercepted 105 drones heading toward the city.
He added that emergency services were working at the debris crash sites but did not provide details on damage or casualties.
Local Telegram channels reported explosions and air defense activity in Domodedovo, Chekhov, Podolsk, and the Stupinsky district.
The Russian Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya) announced that flight operations at Moscow’s Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky airports were temporarily suspended due to the attacks.
This is not the first incident in the area; on July 28, a fire broke out at the nearby Koledino3Pl logistics complex following a drone strike.
Strike on Galaktika shopping center in occupied Donetsk
In a separate development, explosions were reported late Saturday evening, Aug. 15, in occupied Donetsk, with local residents reporting a drone attack.
World Archery Allows Russian Athletes to Compete Under National Flag
According to the Exilenova+ Telegram channel, drones struck the Galaktika shopping center in the city, sparking a large-scale fire.
Russian occupation authorities have not yet issued an official statement regarding the consequences of the attack or potential casualties.
Sustained campaign against Wildberries infrastructure
The Sunday strikes on the Koledino and Domodedovo facilities follow a sustained Ukrainian campaign targeting Wildberries’ logistics and digital infrastructure.
On Aug. 10-11, cyber specialists from Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) attacked the company’s digital infrastructure.
HUR’s Cyber Corps reported that the operation caused large-scale disruptions, affecting the main customer service channel, destabilizing the payment infrastructure, and preventing users from completing financial transactions.
The cyberattack compounds the damage caused by a series of drone strikes.
Since mid-July, Ukraine has targeted at least 23 Wildberries facilities. Data Insight analysts estimate that prior to Sunday’s attacks, the company had already lost up to one-third of its warehouse space (at least 1.18 million square meters), with destroyed or damaged goods valued at approximately 480 billion rubles ($5.7 billion).
The financial losses are roughly equivalent to the annual budgets of wealthier Russian regions like Krasnoyarsk Krai. The disruptions have significantly impacted tens of thousands of businesses reliant on the platform, which accounts for approximately 10% of Russia’s retail sales.
Kyiv has stated that Wildberries is a legitimate military target, asserting that the marketplace sells goods used by the Russian armed forces. While the company denies supplying the military, reports indicate that dual-use items such as first-person-view (FPV) drones and fiber-optic cables were available for purchase on the platform in early August.

articles.title: North Korea, Russia reaffirm ties on Korean Liberation Day, as Kim sends Putin more troops
articles.body:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un reaffirmed the deepening of ties with Russia in a message to President Vladimir Putin as Pyongyang marked the anniversary of independence from Japan's colonial rule, KCNA state news agency said on Sunday.
Kim was replying to a message of congratulations from Putin marking Saturday's 81st anniversary of Tokyo's surrender in World War Two. The Russian leader said the bond was forged as Soviet soldiers fought against Japan and that cooperation would continue "in all the sectors."
The North Korean leader expressed hope for the future of ties that had "carried forward the history of common struggle for justice and precious traditions of friendship."
Pyongyang and Moscow have grown closer since the reclusive state began deploying troops and weapons to support Russia's war against Ukraine in what has been Pyongyang's most significant involvement in a war since the 1950s.
The Russian ship Pallada arrived at Wonsan port for a goodwill visit on Saturday tied to the liberation anniversary, and was greeted by North Korean provincial officials and Russian embassy staff, KCNA said.
South Korean President calls for talks
Also on Saturday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called for talks with the rival North aimed at peaceful coexistence, telling Seoul's Liberation Day ceremony that the two Koreas need safeguards to prevent conflict and should work to replace their armistice with a "peace regime."
Lee urged dialogue to formally end the 1950-1953 Korean War, which ended in a ceasefire but no peace treaty, and said the talks could explore ways to curb Pyongyang's nuclear program.
Pyongyang has rejected Lee's overtures and criticized US-South Korean military exercises as provocations.
On Thursday, Putin drew Tokyo's condemnation with a visit to an island off Hokkaido, claimed by Japan, that Moscow seized in the days after Japan's 1945 surrender.

articles.title: Why Iran’s threat keeps haunting the Middle East - and how to finally break the cycle - opinion
articles.body:
For nearly 50 years, the world has dealt with Iran under a straightforward premise: the sole source of danger is the theocracy installed by the 1979 revolution.
Western policies have split between containing the regime, changing its conduct, eroding its capabilities, or waiting for internal collapse. The record of these tactics, though, raises a tougher question.
Why does the Iranian threat return each time Tehran’s foes believe they have contained it?
The breeding grounds enabling centralized power
For decades, the world may have fixated on who governs Iran while ignoring the framework that lets central authorities rebuild their power project whenever conditions change.
The core issue is about more than the nuclear program, ballistic missile stockpile, and proxy networks. These are assets that can be disabled or partly destroyed.
They spring, however, from a large state with a huge population, energy reserves, a scientific and industrial foundation, geographic reach, and military institutions honed across decades.
Lost facilities, leaders, and munitions cannot wipe out technical know-how or erase recovery capacity. A single tool may break, but the underlying machine still can build a replacement.
History shows international dealings with Iran have targeted what can be destroyed; capabilities can be degraded. But such tactics leave unanswered the more fundamental question of how to stop a large, centralized state with people, resources and expertise from rebuilding losses once conditions ease.
So, the issue moves from disarmament to state structure, from who governs Iran to how power sources inside the country are administered.
One episode lays bare this disconnect. The July 2015 nuclear deal capped portions of Iran’s nuclear work. It left Tehran’s view of its regional standing intact. Missile work and proxy operations also proceeded without pause.
The January 2020 killing of Maj.-Gen. Qasem Soleimani jolted the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, although influence networks resumed activity once roles were reassigned.
Strikes on Iranian military sites have proved able to inflict damage and disrupt operations, but they cannot ensure permanent disablement.
Containment thus amounts to little more than managing repeated rounds of buildup, strike and rearmament.
Viewed this way, regime change in Iran offers at best a partial fix if presented as a final answer to the problem. The ruling system provides the country’s power project with its ideology, while the centralized state furnishes its resources and wealth.
Replacing the regime while leaving power administration untouched may soften rhetoric but offers no assurance of a different course. A more pragmatic, economy-focused government could emerge.
Geography, national interests and latent capabilities, however, survive leadership turnover. Long-held regional ambitions would likely resurface, framed in nationalist rather than revolutionary terms.
That said, casting the Iranian state as inherently hostile misreads reality. Most countries adjust conduct when their institutions, military doctrine, and balance between rulers and ruled evolve.
The objective is something other than indefinite weakening of Iran. It is blocking the convergence of unchecked central power, expansionist ideology, and exclusive control over military decisions.
Chaotic breakup of the Iranian state carries its own severe risks. Internal diversity, widespread weapons, and Iran’s strategic position could turn collapse into civil conflict, foreign meddling, and massive disruption of energy flows and shipping lanes.
Break the ‘buildup, strike, resurgence’ pattern
The most durable course therefore starts inside Iran, on the premise that Iranians alone hold the right to choose their governing system and its structure.
Broad decentralization or federalism, and possibly confederal arrangements if adopted through national consent and constitutional agreement, can curb the center’s monopoly on wealth and decisions, give regions greater say over resources and fiscal matters, and write institutional limits into the use of national capacities for foreign ventures.
Forcing such models from outside, by contrast, would let authorities cast themselves as defenders of national unity and turn reform into a pretext for harsher repression.
Decentralization hardly guarantees Iran will turn automatically into a peaceful country. Constitutional arrangements by themselves cannot dispel national ambitions or remove foreign frictions. Their worth lies in raising the price of decision monopolization, spreading oversight of resources, and making long-term foreign ventures far harder to pursue without broad consent and accountability.
Such rules constrain impulsive action while still falling short of an ironclad promise of responsible behavior.
No global requirement exists for a permanent Iranian adversary to justify alliances and defense budgets. Removing the regime with no plan for what follows promises an even more dangerous crisis.
What is required instead is ending the threat’s ability to regenerate, through four parallel steps: capping offensive capabilities, advancing institutional reform that disperses power inside Iran, upholding regional deterrence to block coercion, and pursuing diplomacy that links economic and political integration to revised conduct.
The world has repeatedly slowed Iran’s power project. It has never eliminated the country’s ability to rebuild it. The ruling system may fall one day, but its collapse would leave intact the building blocks of Iranian strength.
If a framework survives that lets central authorities marshal people, resources and expertise behind foreign ventures, any win will amount to a temporary pause between rounds.
A credible resolution comes when Iran’s strength changes from a source of fear for neighbors into a force bounded by institutions and directed by societal interests. Only then does the root problem resolve itself. The danger will not have sustained another setback – it will have lost the conditions that kept reviving it.
The writer is a UAE political analyst and former Federal National Council candidate.

articles.title: Russian Strikes Devastate Metinvest’s Zaporizhstal Factory, Epicentr Mall in Zaporizhzhia

articles.title: Africa's low-key high-stakes Strait of Hormuz diplomacy
articles.body:
Africa's low-key high-stakes Strait of Hormuz diplomacy
August 16, 2026
One of the principal arteries of world trade has been chronically blocked for almost six months. Maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has been reduced to a bare minimum since the first US-Israeli airstrikes on Iran at the end of February. Cargo ships have at times been fired on by Iranian forces; at others, threats from Tehran or Washington have been enough to bring shipping to a standstill.
So far, various rounds of talks, a joint memorandum and third-party deliberations about the creation of a maritime mission have not succeeded in stabilizing the situation. It remains to be seen whether a deal between Iran and Oman on establishing a shipping route through the strait will do so.
The war has prompted fossil fuel prices to soar all over the world, with inflation rising as a result. Despite its relative proximity to the Gulf region, some parts of Africa have experienced serious shortages because of the bottlenecks, with long lines of cars at gas stations that have run out of fuel. As many fertilizers are also sourced from the Gulf region, this year's harvests also threaten to be bad. African governments therefore have every reason to engage diplomatically in finding a permanent solution.
Cautious diplomacy
"I believe their long-term plan is still based on the assumption that the crisis in the Middle East may continue for some time," says Liesl Louw-Vaudran from the International Crisis Group, an NGO that works to prevent conflicts.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June, but Louw-Vaudran, an expert advisor working with the African Union, comments: "We don't see any evidence that there was some kind of optimism or revising of any economic planning after the MOU. I think everyone literally is just waiting to see how this is going to pan out in the next couple of months."
It's certainly the case that a low-key approach has dominated African diplomacy with regard to Hormuz in recent months. There have been numerous calls for negotiated solutions, praise for diplomatic initiatives and an emphasis on the rules-based order. Some African governments have also shown solidarity with the Arab Gulf states, which, as US allies, have come under fire from Iran.
The current African members of the UN Security Council — the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Somalia and Liberia — also backed a UN resolution adopted in March that strongly condemned Iranian attacks on the Gulf states.
The elephant in the room: Donald Trump
However, it is apparent from their communications that African governments are trying to avoid apportioning blame — especially to the US president, who, together with Israeli president Benjamin Netanyahu, was the one who started the war.
"Every rational human being in the world knows that this crisis has been occasioned by Mr. Donald Trump," says Dismas Mokua, a political risk analyst with the Kenyan advisory firm Tricarta. "But the majority of African leaders, and indeed across the world, fear to call him out because of the consequences. And I've seen European leaders tiptoeing around this issue, I've seen leaders from Asia — leaders all over the world. I've not seen a single leader who has come out to call Mr. Trump, because I guess they fear the consequences of their speech."
What if the whole of Africa were to speak with one voice — perhaps through the African Union? Louw-Vaudran from the International Crisis Group thinks a recent negative experience is still too fresh.
"The African Union Commission in Addis Ababa burned its fingers in the early days of the Ukraine war, in 2022, when the previous chairperson criticized Russia. And heads of state then immediately silenced him, and said that the commission doesn't have the mandate to speak on foreign affairs issues on behalf of the continent," Louw-Vaudran says.
She points out that the AU, with 55 member states, is "very much divided," and says that, since then, "when it comes to political statements in this big, rapidly changing geopolitical situation, the commission has been hesitant."
Ease the symptoms, don't create new problems
The crisis also requires governments to take action rather than just make statements.
"For most countries, or even companies, to be successful wherever there is a disruption in this global supply, you have to reevaluate your supply chains and find out which fits your interest," Mokua says. "And in my view, Kenya has managed to do that with a lot of success."
He comments that he hasn't seen anyone — and, in particular, commercial farmers — complaining about deliveries.
"And even for the supply of oil and gas products, people anticipated that there were going to be shortages. But there were no shortages. The suppliers have been constant and reliable, despite the increase in cost."
But the experience of neighboring Ethiopia has been very different. Delivery bottlenecks forced the government to temporarily prioritize security agencies, public transport and agriculture when distributing fuel. Private individuals were stuck waiting at empty gas stations.
Before the war, Ethiopia was one of Iran's most important African trading partners. That connection is now also at risk, since Ethiopia also relies on maintaining good relations with the United Arab Emirates and increasingly with Saudi Arabia, too.
Countries like Ethiopia and Kenya may also be about to feel another, delayed effect of the Iran war. If the rich Gulf states' economies falter, East African migrant workers there will transfer less money back home.
Opportunity for African countries to work together
But there are also some African countries for whom the uncertain situation in the Gulf might actually be helpful. Nigeria's huge new Dangote refinery came online at just the right time. Intended to ease fuel shortages in the oil-rich country, it's now a mainstay of the world market. In April, the refinery became the world's largest exporter of aviation fuel.
Responding to the Hormuz crisis, Nigeria has offered itself as a partner for African clients. The Dangote corporation is already planning another refinery in Kenya. And the government is standing with the Gulf states: On the oil market, countries seek to be partners, not competitors.
"Nigeria has been very smart, at least in terms of that economic positioning, having the crude itself," says Liesl Louw-Vaudran. "But obviously Nigeria has got huge governance and security issues that are very difficult to overcome."
Perhaps the least visible issue in the short term but one that is likely to have the most lasting impact: The crisis provides another argument for pressing ahead with the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
"There are a number of countries that do not understand the meaning of dismantling these artificial borders. They fear that they are going to lose political control," says the analyst Dismas Mokua.
But he added that he believes many African countries will eventually embrace the dismantling of arbitrary borders drawn up by European colonizers at the infamous Berlin Conference in 1885. "If you want to immunize yourself from the vagaries associated with the global disruption, then you must learn to trade within Africa," he says.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: NATO fighter jet shoots down drone in Romania near border with Ukraine
articles.body:
NATO fighter jet shoots down drone in Romania near border with Ukraine
Romania's defense ministry said Sunday a NATO fighter jet shot down a drone that had entered its airspace near the border with two of its neighboring countries Ukraine and Moldova.
The ministry said in a statement the drone had entered from Moldova and was intercepted by an Spanish F-18 jet deployed on NATO duties early Sunday morning. Debris fell in an unpopulated area near the border with Ukraine, the ministry added.
The interception is the latest in a series of similar recurring incidents involving drones straying into Ukraine's neighboring countries borders, which authorities have blamed on electronic interference as part of the war with Russia. In some cases, the drones are Ukrainian and are "hijacked" by Russian forces.
Authorities have reported finding drone fragments on Romanian soil several times since 2023 following Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports along the Danube River, which lie just across the border. Last week, Ukraine denied targeting Bulgaria after a drone entered the country's airspace on Saturday and exploded close to an international gas pipeline shortly after crossing the border from Romania.
Last month, Romania shot down a drone for the first time since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, after it entered the country's airspace about 60 miles from Bucharest.
In June, Latvia's military said two NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered the country's airspace. Ukrainian drones have previously crashed in all three Baltic states, which all share borders with Russia, with officials blaming the inadvertent incursion on Russian electronic warfare.

articles.title: Taiwan tracks 11 Chinese military aircraft and 10 ships
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked 11 Chinese military aircraft, eight naval vessels, and two official ships between 6 a.m. on Saturday and the same time Sunday.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems. Seven of the People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s northern and central air defense identification zones, or ADIZ, according to the ministry.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese military aircraft 126 times and ships 189 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around Taiwan.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

articles.title: South Korea fired warning shots after North Korean soldiers crossed demarcation line
articles.body:
South Korea's military last week fired warning shots after North Korean soldiers violated the military demarcation line, prompting them to return, Yonhap news agency reported on Sunday, citing an unnamed source.
Yonhap said multiple North Korean soldiers crossed the military demarcation line (MDL) in the eastern area of the demilitarised zone (DMZ), in the first reported MDL violation by the North Korean military this year.
The soldiers were likely patrolling the area when they crossed the MDL, and no other unusual activity was reported after the North Korean soldiers returned, Yonhap said.
The North Korean embassy in Singapore did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
North Korean troops violated the MDL 17 times last year, the news agency said.
The two Koreas are still technically at war after their 1950-53 war ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty.
It comes as North Korea denounced upcoming joint military drills by tens of thousands of US and South Korean forces, warning it could respond with stronger deterrence measures.
The 11-day exercises due to begin on Monday are a regular fixture of the summer calendar, designed to prepare the United States and South Korea to defend against the nuclear-armed North.

articles.title: US Representative McCaul warns warns of China's belligerence toward Taiwan
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — US Rep. Michael McCaul, chair emeritus of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, warned that China's increasingly belligerent threats toward Taiwan pose a direct challenge to the global balance of power during his third visit to Taiwan, per VOA.
McCaul, a Republican from Texas, visited Taiwan from Aug. 2-7, meeting with President Lai Ching-te (賴清德), Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴), and Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍). He also delivered a speech at the annual Ketagalan Forum, where he reiterated US support under the Taiwan Relations Act.
"At a time when the stakes couldn't be higher, I was proud to visit Taiwan for the third time to reaffirm the United States' unwavering support," McCaul said in a statement. "The increasing belligerence of the Chinese Communist Party poses a direct threat — not only to Taiwan, but to the entire global balance of power," per a press release.
McCaul said he has consistently supported Taiwan, including efforts to advance the 2024 Supplemental Appropriations Act and strengthen US-Taiwan economic relations. He also highlighted his support for closer security cooperation among the US, Australia, and the United Kingdom. In recognition of his support for Taiwan, Lai awarded McCaul the Grand Cordon of the Order of the Brilliant Star.
McCaul previously announced that he would not seek reelection after his current term in Congress expires.
During his visit, McCaul also met with opposition leaders, including Legislative Yuan Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), and legislators from opposition parties. Discussions covered Taiwan's recently passed defense budget, the importance of drones, and US-Taiwan cooperation on drone production.
Before leaving Taiwan, McCaul also met with officials from the National Security Council and Ministry of National Defense to exchange views on strengthening Taiwan's defenses against China's coercive actions in the region. He also visited US drone company Shield AI and the Industrial Technology Research Institute, where he learned about Taiwan's drone industry and ITRI's certification work.
ITRI is the first institution outside the US authorized to certify that drones do not contain components from China, per VOA.
McCaul, a member of the House of Representatives Taiwan Caucus, first visited Taiwan in April 2023 as chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. He returned in May 2024 to attend Lai's inauguration.
China conducted military exercises involving aircraft and naval forces around Taiwan during both of those visits and imposed sanctions on McCaul. During his latest visit, McCaul said China's coercive actions had only strengthened his commitment to supporting a free and peaceful Taiwan.

articles.title: ‘No Room for Mistakes’: What Next for Protestors Demanding Fedorov’s Reinstatement?
articles.body:
On Sunday Aug. 16, a significant rally in support of Mykhailo Fedorov, along with a demand for the continuation of reforms at the Ministry of Defense, is due to take place in central Kyiv. However, the focus of recent protests is already shifting beyond these boundaries, with many of the banners and placards no longer mentioning Fedorov.

At the Aug. 14 rally, broader grievances against the authorities came to the fore – corruption, non-transparent decision-making, not listening to the people, and even the cutting down of 100-year-old oak trees in one of Kyiv’s districts for the benefit of developers, which has stirred anger among local residents.
                                                                                                                                                                         
One of the main slogans of last week’s large march, which gathered more than 10,000 people, was “Listening to the people – that’s powerful,” where the word “powerful,” which President Volodymyr Zelensky had previously used extensively, was employed as a form of trolling.
Zelensky Confirms Flamingo Missile Strikes Deep in Russian Territory
However, the future of the rallies is now very much in question.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Many commentators believe that, despite the uncertainty surrounding Fedorov himself (he said that negotiations with representatives of the authorities are still ongoing), President Zelensky is unlikely to be considering the option of returning him to the position of head of the Ministry of Defense.
Why?
First, General Yevhenii Khmara has already been introduced to key players and foreign partners as acting minister of defense; and second, the president cannot risk showing to the hierarchy that he is willing to give in to the street on everything.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The situation is made even more uncertain by Fedorov himself. He has not come out to the people on Maidan – that would have meant his transition into active politics – and he has indicated a lack of desire to criticize President Zelensky until the end of the war.
In a conversation with prominent civic activist Serhiy Sternenko, Fedorov said: “I will not lead the protest, because it will be perceived as a political move. And our task is to win the war.”
According to several journalists and political strategists, this is a mistake.
Ukrainian journalist Maryna Danyliuk-Yermolayeva stated. “Yes, Yushchenko’s emergence among the wider masses as a talented economist turned him into an icon of the national democrats. Yulia Tymoshenko’s appearances among the people cemented her for a long time as the people’s darling, the princess of Ukrainian politics. The same ride on a road grader by Petro Poroshenko at the dawn of the Revolution of Dignity instantly propelled the former minister in Azarov’s government to the top of the ratings… Fedorov said in an interview with The New York Times that he would not be in opposition until the end of the war. But it is worth saying that after that there will be new heroes. And they will certainly know how to go out into the streets and meet with people.”
The future of the protests therefore look ambiguous.
The largest rally, “The Last Attempt to Reach the President,” is due to take place on Sunday Aug. 16. On Tuesday Aug. 18, during parliament’s plenary week, lawmakers will vote for the new head of the Ministry of Defense.
Will the rallies continue if it becomes clear that Fedorov will definitely not return to his former ministerial post?
And if they do continue, how long can they last?
For now, this question remains open. All the more so because the main grievance of part of society toward Zelensky is not so much about Fedorov as it is about the systemic problems that forced Zelensky to dismiss the defense minister – even knowing that this would cause dissatisfaction.

articles.title: The 1991 treaty that still haunts the Kremlin
articles.body:
As Russia wages war on Ukraine, denying its own history of aggression against its neighbours, a little-known treaty signed 35 years ago is quietly getting in the way of the Kremlin's narrative.
In July 1991, five months before the Soviet Union formally dissolved, Russia signed a treaty with Lithuania in which it recognised something Moscow has spent the past two decades trying to erase from the record: that the Soviet Union illegally annexed Lithuania in 1940, and that Lithuania's independence, declared in 1990, was legitimate.
That document is still in force. Russia has never torn it up. And that, say Lithuanian officials and legal experts, makes it an awkward loose end for a Kremlin that now insists the Baltic states were never really occupied at all.
Under President Vladimir Putin, Russian state doctrine has increasingly leaned on the claim that the Baltic states joined the USSR voluntarily, and that talk of "occupation" is Western-backed revisionism.
That framing underpins not only Moscow's rhetoric towards Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia but also, in a broader sense, the ideological justification for its invasion of Ukraine – the idea that the borders and independence of post-Soviet states are negotiable, or fictional.
The 1991 treaty directly contradicts that. Dainius Žalimas, a Lithuanian MEP who has studied the treaty closely, argues that its first article, which has no expiry date, remains one of Lithuania's strongest legal cards: it commits both countries to recognising each other as sovereign states with an inalienable right to independence, and bars either from meddling in each other's internal affairs as well as using or threatening force against the other.
"All of this essentially refutes every claim made by current official Russian propaganda, and undermines the very foundations of the ideology of 'rashism'. That ideology, which underpins both the aggression against Ukraine and the denial of Baltic statehood, recognises neither the occupation of Lithuania nor the continuity of the Lithuanian state, among much else," said Žalimas.
"I think the treaty is very important. We talk about the wavering authority of international law, but it gives Lithuania a solid line of international legal defence, and shows that Russia, for very brief periods in its history, can be different," he added.
For example, Lithuania can continue to demand compensation from Russia for the damage caused by occupation, even though few believe this will ever happen in practice.
"Just as the treaty of July 12, 1920 formed the basis for all subsequent treaties with the Soviet Union, the same applies here – dozens of Lithuanian-Russian agreements rest on the July 29, 1991 treaty. So the treaty still holds, as long as they haven't broken it," explained Česlovas Vytautas Stankevičius, former deputy chairman of the Supreme Council and head of the negotiating delegation with Russia, highlighting why the treaty still carries weight to this day.
How it came about
The path to the treaty began in secrecy. In May 1990, Vytautas Landsbergis, then chairman of Lithuania's Supreme Council (the country's parliament in the final Soviet years), held a clandestine meeting with Boris Yeltsin, his Russian counterpart, in an empty Moscow school classroom. The two men barely knew each other personally, and the meeting was arranged through informal contacts.
Two months later, leaders of the three Baltic states and Russia met in the Latvian town of Jūrmala and agreed to pursue bilateral treaties – partly as a way of applying pressure on Mikhail Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, who was still trying to hold the union together.
That effort was not merely symbolic. The USSR spent 1990 and 1991 trying to force Lithuania, as well as other republics, back into line, including a 75-day economic blockade after its declaration of independence.
At the time, it was unclear whether it was better to negotiate with the Soviet leadership or with Russia, which in June 1990 had issued its own declaration of state sovereignty. As a result, negotiations proceeded with both the Soviet authorities and with Yeltsin's Russia, which proved to be a great decision since once the Soviet Union collapsed, Russia became its legal successor.
For Lithuania, negotiating and signing the treaty meant securing the backing of the largest Soviet republic for its independence – a powerful argument against the Soviet Union. Meanwhile, Russia's leadership was competing during with the central Soviet authorities for control.
"The goals of the two states coincided," summarized Stankevičius, who was appointed head of Lithuania's negotiating delegation.
Having concluded treaties with Latvia and Estonia, Russia wanted to sign a similar document with Lithuania.
But Lithuania's treaty took longer to conclude, largely because Vilnius pushed for tougher language than Moscow wanted to accept.
The sticking points
Negotiators clashed over three issues in particular.
The first was citizenship. Lithuania wanted to prevent members of the Soviet military and security apparatus – as well as their families – from automatically qualifying for Lithuanian citizenship, while also avoiding a settlement that would let ethnic Russians resident in the country claim dual nationality.
A compromise formula eventually restricted citizenship rights to those with ties to Russia who had lived and worked in Lithuania since before November 1989.
The second was how to characterise the movement of people under Soviet rule – specifically, how to avoid a formula that would have put Lithuanians deported to Russia by Stalin's regime in the same legal category as Russians who had been resettled into Lithuania as part of Soviet colonisation policy.
The two sides eventually agreed on the neutral term "relocating persons" to cover both groups without equating them politically.
Finally, the thorniest question – whether Russia would accept responsibility for the 1940 annexation – was resolved not by the negotiating teams but by Landsbergis and Yeltsin personally.
"The Russian negotiators didn't want to accept responsibility for crimes committed by the Bolsheviks – all those acts of violence and coercion against neighbouring states. They didn't want the responsibility. Their position was that the Russian Federation, in restoring its own statehood, would not take on responsibility for the crimes of the communist regime," Stankevičius told LRT.lt.
Meanwhile, Landsbergis's own public position at the time was that responsibility lay with the USSR rather than Russia specifically.
So, the compromise text kept a reference to the 1940 annexation while dropping Lithuania's request to invoke an earlier, 1920 peace treaty in which Soviet Russia had renounced all claims to Lithuanian territory, making it's later Soviet occupation – illegal.
The irony
That compromise proved more significant than either side may have anticipated. When the Soviet Union collapsed months later, Russia inherited its rights and obligations as successor state – including, Lithuanian officials argue, responsibility for the consequences of the 1940 annexation that Russia itself had just agreed to acknowledge. And so, it was obliged to remedy the damage, withdraw its troops, and so on.
Three and a half decades on, the treaty's core value lies precisely in the fact that it is Moscow's own signature on a document that says the opposite of what the Kremlin now claims.

JERUSALEM, Aug. 16 (Xinhua) -- An Israeli airstrike killed a senior commander in Hezbollah's Badr regional division in southern Lebanon, the Israeli military said Sunday. Lebanese media reported that at least four people were killed in the attack.
The Israeli military said in a statement that Abu Hassan Alaa was killed late on Saturday in the strike on Deir al-Zahrani. It described the attack as "a response" to an earlier Hezbollah drone strike targeting Israeli troops in southern Lebanon that wounded three soldiers.
Lebanon's state-run National News Agency said Israeli warplanes struck a two-story building, killing at least four people and wounding five.

articles.body:
ALBAWABA - Romania’s Defence Ministry said on Sunday that a drone illegally entered its airspace but was shot down by NATO.
According to the ministry's statement, a drone illegally breached Romania's national airspace, and it was destroyed by a Spanish F-18 fighter jet pilot at 05:01 a.m., CNN reported.
The F-18 jet "made radar contact with the target and received permission to engage it," the ministry revealed Sunday.

articles.title: Taichung uses AI cameras, drones to crack down on illegal open burning
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung’s Environmental Protection Bureau said Saturday that its artificial intelligence camera system and aerial drones have detected hundreds of cases of illegal open burning, resulting in NT$1.28 million (US$39,000) in fines, according to a Taichung City Government press release.
The bureau said it began deploying AI smoke-detecting cameras along with drones in 2022. When the camera system detects abnormal air pollution, it alerts authorities, who then deploy drones and send inspectors to the location.
The bureau said the ground-and-air surveillance network has caught hundreds of cases of unauthorized open burning, with fines totaling NT$1.28 million. The bureau added that nearly 170 AI smoke-detection systems have been installed across Taichung to improve enforcement efficiency.
The bureau said open burning harms air quality and may cause fires. Under the Air Pollution Control Act, violators can be fined up to NT$100,000, while industrial or commercial facilities can face fines of up to NT$5 million, the bureau said.

articles.title: Iran says Qatar delaying probe into fate of Iranian pilots, Tasnim news agency
articles.body:
Iran disputes Qatar, Kuwait accounts of captured Iranian personnel
DUBAI, Aug 16 - An Iranian military official said on Sunday that Qatar should allow an Iranian team to enter the country to investigate the fate of pilots whom Tehran says were captured by Qatari forces, Iranian media reported.
Qatar denies holding any Iranian pilots. Doha said on Saturday that its search and rescue teams had found the remains of one pilot after Iranian aircraft violated Qatari airspace in March and failed to respond to attempts to contact them.
Qatar said it had contacted Iran to coordinate the handover of the remains and had invited Tehran to review details of its search and rescue operations, but had received no response.
Mohammad Baqerzadeh, commander of the Committee for the Search for Missing Persons of Iran's Armed Forces General Staff, said an Iranian Air Force expert and fact-finding team had been waiting for months to enter Qatar, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Baqerzadeh accused Qatari officials of repeatedly delaying the investigation and preventing the pilots' return to Iran. He called for the International Committee of the Red Cross to urgently follow up on the case.
Baqerzadeh also said Kuwait was similarly withholding information about the fate of four Iranians held in Kuwait.
In May, Iran said the four were affiliated with the Revolutionary Guards and had been on a maritime patrol before entering Kuwaiti territorial waters because of a navigation disruption. Kuwait has said the four were suspected of planning hostile actions against the country. REUTERS

articles.title: Morocco arrests more than 100 people near Ceuta border
articles.body:
Moroccan police arrested at least 111 people attempting to reach the Spanish territory of Ceuta on Saturday after calls circulated on social media for another mass border crossing. Authorities in Morocco and Spain deployed security forces around the border following the arrival of tens of thousands of people in Ceuta two weeks earlier.
A Moroccan Interior Ministry source told Reuters that 109 of those detained were migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and two were Moroccan citizens.
The arrests took place in and around Fnideq, a coastal town about three kilometres from the Ceuta border.
Groups travelled through hills outside Fnideq in an apparent effort to avoid security checkpoints. Spanish news agency EFE reported that Moroccan police used tear gas to disperse people gathered in the area.
Reuters later saw hundreds of Moroccan officers returning from the hills, including police in riot equipment and plain-clothes personnel.
The official arrest figure differed from figures reported by Moroccan media. Local outlet Le360 put the number at 294, including 46 Moroccans. Authorities had not confirmed that higher figure.
Morocco increased security after online messages called for a mass crossing on 15 August. The government said earlier in the week that it was monitoring posts of unknown origin and warned that organisers and participants faced prosecution.
Moroccan forces deployed police, military personnel, naval vessels and drones near the border. Authorities also established checkpoints and prevented some groups from taking trains and buses towards northern Morocco.
Spain increased its presence on the other side of the border. More than 1,600 police officers were deployed in Ceuta after Madrid sent over 500 additional officers from mainland Spain, Reuters reported. Spain also installed a maritime barrier following the previous influx.
The security operation followed a mass arrival on 30 July, when more than 72,000 people entered Ceuta.
At least 96 people died during the crossing, according to Reuters.
Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said on Thursday that about 5,000 migrants remained in Ceuta. He said people who entered without authorisation would not be transferred to mainland Spain or granted legal status except in cases involving vulnerability. Those without a right to remain would face return to Morocco.
The July arrivals also led to disputes between European Union states. Italy introduced border controls on arrivals from Spain, citing migration concerns. Spain responded with controls of its own after asking Rome to withdraw the measure.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on Saturday that Italy had feared another large arrival in Ceuta.
“We're not waging any kind of ‘battle’ against Spain,” Tajani said. “We're simply carefully controlling arrivals.”
Ceuta lies on the North African coast and shares a land border with Morocco. Spain administers the territory, while Morocco disputes Spanish sovereignty over the enclave.

articles.title: Ukraine’s  Mahuchikh Wins Third Consecutive European High Jump Gold
articles.body:
Ukrainian athlete Yaroslava Mahuchikh won the gold medal in the women’s high jump at the 2026 European Athletics Championships in Birmingham, England, clearing a height of 1.97 meters, Ukrinform reported.
Mahuchikh entered the competition at 1.92 meters, clearing the bar on her first attempt. She required a second attempt to clear 1.95 meters.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Fellow Ukrainian Iryna Herashchenko, who had cleared 1.83 meters, 1.88 meters, and 1.92 meters, failed to clear 1.95 meters and finished in fifth place.
With the bar raised to 1.97 meters, Mahuchikh cleared the height on her first attempt, securing the gold medal. She subsequently made three unsuccessful attempts at 2.01 meters.
Poland’s Maria Zhodzik secured the silver medal, and Montenegro’s Marija Vukovic took bronze. Both athletes cleared 1.95 meters but failed all three attempts at 1.97 meters.
The victory in Birmingham marks Mahuchikh’s third consecutive European Championship title, following her wins in 2022 and 2024.
According to Suspilne Sport, Mahuchikh tied the record for the most European Championship titles in the high jump.
With this victory, Mahuchikh tied the record set by Spain’s Ruth Beitia, who had previously been the only athlete to become a three-time European champion in the high jump. She won three consecutive gold medals in 2012, 2014, and 2016.
Beitia also became an Olympic champion in 2016, but she never won a world championship. Mahuchikh won gold at the 2023 World Championships.

Mahuchikh’s European title follows her gold medal victory at the World Indoor Championships in Toruń, Poland, in March, where she cleared 2.01 meters. Ukrainian athlete Yuliia Levchenko secured silver at the same event with a jump of 1.99 meters.
These athletic achievements occur against the backdrop of ongoing debates regarding the participation of athletes from Russia and Belarus in international sports.
In February, the International Paralympic Committee allowed a limited number of Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in the 2026 Games under their national flags.
Separately, the International Olympic Committee disqualified Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych from the 2026 Winter Olympics after he refused to remove a helmet depicting Ukrainian athletes killed during the war.
